title: Objective-C tutorial: messages, classes, Foundation collections and blocks — cv.cm
description: Learn Objective-C basics: compile Hello world with clang, send messages, define classes and properties, use NSArray and NSDictionary, blocks, ARC and NSError.
answer: Objective-C is C with Smalltalk-style object-oriented messaging added on top. You call methods by sending messages in square brackets, `[object doSomething:arg]`, define classes in `@interface` and `@implementation` blocks, and use Apple's Foundation framework for strings, arrays and dictionaries. It was the main language for macOS and iOS apps before Swift and is still used in many existing Apple code bases. On a Mac, compile with `clang -fobjc-arc -framework Foundation hello.m`.

sections.h: What Objective-C is and who uses it
body: Objective-C was created by Brad Cox and Tom Love in the early 1980s, adopted by NeXT for its NeXTSTEP system, and inherited by Apple, where NeXTSTEP became the basis of macOS and iOS. It is a strict superset of C: any C code is valid Objective-C, and you can mix the two freely.

Today Apple recommends Swift for new apps, but Objective-C remains fully supported. It is found in older iOS and macOS apps, in many system frameworks and third-party libraries, and in projects that mix C or C++ with Apple APIs. Swift and Objective-C interoperate in the same project, so knowing both is useful for Apple platform developers.

On macOS, install Xcode or only the command line tools (`xcode-select --install`), which include the clang compiler and the Foundation framework. Source files use the `.m` extension; headers use `.h`.

body.code:
clang -fobjc-arc -framework Foundation hello.m -o hello
./hello
# 2026-10-31 10:00:00.000 hello[1234:5678] Hello, world!

body: `NSLog` writes to standard error and adds a timestamp and process name. `@"..."` creates an `NSString` object instead of a C string. `-fobjc-arc` turns on Automatic Reference Counting, the standard memory management. On Linux, the GNUstep project provides a compatible Foundation library, with different build commands.

Because Objective-C is C, all C types work. Objects are always used through pointers (`NSString *name`). Calling a method is called sending a message; arguments are interleaved with the parts of the method name.

body: In format strings, `%@` prints an object (it calls its `description` method). Sending a message to `nil` is allowed and returns `nil` or 0, which avoids many crashes but can also hide bugs.
Control flow is exactly C: `if`, `else`, `switch`, `for`, `while` and `do ... while`. Objective-C adds fast enumeration with `for ... in` for collections.

A class has a public interface (usually in a `.h` file) and an implementation (in the `.m` file). Instance methods start with `-`, class methods with `+`. `@property` declares a property and generates its getter, setter and a backing variable named with an underscore.

Objects are created in two steps: `alloc` reserves memory and an `init...` method initializes it. The method above is named `initWithName:age:` (the colons are part of the name). Protocols (`@protocol`) play the role of interfaces, and categories let you add methods to existing classes, even `NSString`.

The Foundation framework provides immutable collections and mutable subclasses. Literals make them short to write. Collections hold only objects, so numbers are boxed as `NSNumber`, and `nil` cannot be stored (use `[NSNull null]` instead).

Blocks, written with `^`, are closures: anonymous functions that capture variables from the surrounding scope. Apple APIs use them for callbacks, sorting and asynchronous work with Grand Central Dispatch. The `<NSString *>` parts are lightweight generics that help the compiler and Swift; they are optional.

With ARC, the compiler inserts reference-counting calls for you: an object is freed when no strong reference points to it. You only need to break reference cycles, usually by marking one side `weak` (for example, a delegate property).

Recoverable errors use the `NSError` pattern: a method returns `nil` or `NO` on failure and fills an `NSError` object passed by reference. Exceptions (`@try`, `@catch`, `NSException`) exist, but in Cocoa they signal programmer errors such as an index out of range, not normal failures.

sections.h: A small complete program: word frequencies
body: For a new word, `counts[word]` is `nil`, and `nil.integerValue` returns 0, so the first count becomes 1. The comparator reverses the order to sort by count from high to low, and `printf` prints without the `NSLog` prefix.

body.note: Common beginner mistakes: comparing strings with `==` (it compares pointers; use `isEqualToString:`); forgetting the `@` before a string literal; forgetting the `*` in object declarations; putting `nil` into an array or dictionary literal, which crashes at run time; printing `NSInteger` with `%d` instead of `%ld` and a cast; and compiling without `-fobjc-arc`.

faq.a: Yes, mainly in existing iOS and macOS apps and libraries. Apple recommends Swift for new code, but Objective-C is still supported by Xcode and the Apple SDKs.

faq.q: Should I learn Swift or Objective-C first?
faq.a: For new Apple development, learn Swift first. Learn Objective-C when you need to read or maintain older code, use C or C++ libraries closely, or understand how Apple frameworks work underneath.

faq.q: What do the square brackets mean in Objective-C?
faq.a: They send a message: `[receiver message]` calls the method `message` on the object `receiver`. Arguments follow colons, as in `[dict setObject:value forKey:key]`.
Modern Objective-C uses Automatic Reference Counting (ARC), where the compiler adds retain and release calls. Apple's older garbage collector for macOS was deprecated and is no longer available.
